source.title: Adversarial Weight Perturbation Helps Robust Generalization
source.authors: Dong-Xian Wu; Shu-Tao Xia; Yisen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests relationships between weight-loss-landscape flatness and adversarial robustness gaps. It does not test the claim versions’ natural-label test error or standard train-test generalization gap.
record.gate_note: Results on adversarial robustness and its training-test gap are a related construct. They do not establish natural-label generalization results. Cited results from other work were excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures adversarial robustness and its train–test gap. These are different outcomes from V7's standard generalization gap. Its natural-accuracy tables do not test any of V1–V8's specified comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report a correlation between weight-loss-landscape flatness and robust generalization gaps, and propose AWP to flatten that landscape and improve adversarial robustness across tested settings. Their results also show that excessive perturbation can reduce robustness.
record.recipe_differences: Studies adversarial training and adversarial robustness gaps, using on-the-fly adversarial examples and relative weight perturbations; it does not use the natural-label generalization setups in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship varies over training time and with γ; the authors also report that early stopping can reduce the adversarial gap while leaving training robustness low.

fits_no_version.finding: Flatter magnitude-normalized adversarial weight-loss landscapes accompany smaller robust generalization gaps across checkpoints and adversarial training methods. Strong AWP can further reduce the gap while lowering both training and test robustness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-loss-landscape flatness tracks the adversarial robustness generalization gap; a small gap alone does not ensure high test robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: AWP improves test robustness over a suitable perturbation range, whereas RWP provides little improvement at small perturbations and impairs robustness at large ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial weight perturbation can improve adversarial robustness more effectively than random weight perturbation.

record.problems: The measured generalization gap concerns adversarial robustness, not natural-label error. The landscape evidence is primarily qualitative and shown in figures; the paper reports omitted standard deviations as very small for some tables, but the gap-landscape comparisons have no stated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No natural-label generalization results matching the claim versions. Benchmark robustness and natural accuracy comparisons in Tables 1–5 were omitted because they do not measure the versions’ natural-label generalization gap.

untested.parts: Joint random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects and its interaction with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus standard generalization gaps among similarly low-loss networks, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Magnitude normalization makes the landscape analysis related to V7, but does not make adversarial and standard generalization gaps interchangeable. The natural-accuracy comparisons change AWP or other regularizers rather than the interventions named in V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width beyond interpolation and natural-label test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected natural-label generalization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out natural-label performance.
Large-batch effects on natural-label held-out performance.
Dropout’s effects on natural-label held-out error.
The measured gap is adversarial robustness, not the natural-label train-test error gap specified in the version.
Removing memorized examples and measuring natural-label test accuracy.

rows.subject: PreAct ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Tracked weight-loss-landscape shape and robust generalization gap during vanilla adversarial training.
rows.measure: Relationship between adversarial weight-loss-landscape flatness and robust generalization gap
rows.value: Before the 103-th epoch, the test robustness is close to the training robustness and the landscape is very flat; after the “best,” the gap becomes larger while the landscape becomes sharper.
rows.note: This is an adversarial robustness gap, not a natural-label train-test error gap.
rows.check: The reported association is observed for adversarial loss landscapes and robust generalization gaps; it cannot establish V7's standard-error association.

rows.subject: PreAct ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared weight-loss-landscape shape with robust generalization gaps across adversarial training methods.

conditions.value: vanilla AT, TRADES, MART, RST, AT-ES

rows.measure: Relationship between landscape flatness and robust generalization gap
rows.value: Compared with vanilla AT, all methods have a smaller robust generalization gap and a flatter weight loss landscape.
rows.note: AT-ES had the flattest landscape and smallest gap, but did not obtain the highest test robustness; the authors attribute this to low training robustness.
rows.check: The comparisons concern robust generalization gaps, not V7's standard generalization gap, and do not compare rankings against norm- or margin-based measures.

rows.subject: PreAct ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Varied the AWP weight-perturbation constraint γ and measured landscape shape and robust generalization gap.
rows.measure: Weight-loss-landscape flatness and robust generalization gap
rows.value: As γ grows, the landscape becomes flatter and the robust generalization gap becomes smaller; at γ = 2 × 10−2, the gap is smallest but training/test robustness decreases.
rows.note: The reported gap and robustness are adversarial.
rows.check: This measures an adversarial gap. Within that construct, the flatter-landscape/smaller-gap association persists at large γ; decreased training and test robustness does not make that association partial.

rows.subject: PreAct ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared random weight perturbation (RWP) and adversarial weight perturbation (AWP) by their effects on the landscape and robustness.
rows.baseline: AT-RWP test robustness almost does not improve at γ ≤ 0.3
rows.value: AWP can significantly improve test robustness at γ ∈ [1 × 10−3, 1 × 10−2]; RWP test robustness begins to decrease when γ ≥ 0.6.
rows.note: Adversarial robustness is not a measure of the natural-label generalization gap.
rows.check: This is the proposed method's robustness comparison with RWP, not a claim-testing row. Its value summarizes an AWP γ sweep, so the condition listing only AWP γ = 0.005 is incomplete.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
